::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This is the foundational case of the [Logistic Regression](index.qmd) module: a
**binary** classifier with **two raw features** and a **linear** decision
boundary. Later notes extend it to multi-class (one-vs-rest, one-vs-one,
multinomial/softmax) and to non-linear boundaries via feature expansion.
:::

## Setup

Suppose we need to learn a classifier with two raw features $x_1$ and $x_2$.
There are two classes, $a$ and $b$. Plotting the training data suggests the two
classes are (roughly) linearly separable:

```
x2
│  a a a
│   a a a  a
│  a  a
│  a        b
│       b  b  b
│    b  b  b  b
│       b   b
└───────────────── x1
```

Because a straight line separates the classes well, a **linear function of the
raw features** is enough — we don't need feature expansion here. So the model has
a weight vector

$$
\mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} w_0 \\ w_1 \\ w_2 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

We build a feature matrix for the $n$ training points, with a leading column of
$1$'s for the bias term $w_0$:

$$
X =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_1^{(1)} & x_2^{(1)} \\
1 & x_1^{(2)} & x_2^{(2)} \\
1 & x_1^{(3)} & x_2^{(3)} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
1 & x_1^{(n)} & x_2^{(n)}
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
X\mathbf{w} = \hat{\mathbf{y}}.
$$

For a single sample it is convenient to write the linear score as

$$
h^{(i)} \;=\; \mathbf{x}^{(i)} \cdot \mathbf{w} \;=\; w_0 + w_1 x_1^{(i)} + w_2 x_2^{(i)}.
$$

## From linear score to probability: the sigmoid

A linear score lives on $(-\infty, \infty)$, but we want a probability in
$[0, 1]$. We pass the score through the **sigmoid** function:

$$
g(h) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-h}}.
$$

We interpret $g(h^{(i)})$ as $P\big(y^{(i)} = 1 \mid \mathbf{w}\big)$, the
probability that sample $i$ belongs to the positive class.

::: {.callout-tip title="Useful identity"}
The sigmoid has a very clean derivative, which is what makes the gradient tidy:

$$
g'(h) = g(h)\,\big(1 - g(h)\big).
$$
:::

## Likelihood

Assuming the training samples are independent, the likelihood (the joint
probability of the observed labels) is the product over all samples:

$$
P = \prod_{i=1}^{n}
\underbrace{P\big(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{w}\big)^{\,y^{(i)}}}_{\text{when } y^{(i)}=1}
\cdot
\underbrace{P\big(y = 0 \mid \mathbf{w}\big)^{\,(1 - y^{(i)})}}_{\text{when } y^{(i)}=0}.
$$

Substituting the sigmoid:

$$
P = \prod_{i=1}^{n}
\left( \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w_0 + w_1 x_1^{(i)} + w_2 x_2^{(i)})}} \right)^{y^{(i)}}
\cdot
\left( 1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w_0 + w_1 x_1^{(i)} + w_2 x_2^{(i)})}} \right)^{(1 - y^{(i)})}.
$$

## Log-likelihood

Taking logs turns the product into a sum (and is numerically nicer):

$$
\ln(P) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
y^{(i)} \ln\!\big(g(h^{(i)})\big)
+ \big(1 - y^{(i)}\big) \ln\!\big(1 - g(h^{(i)})\big)
\right].
$$

## Objective (loss) function

We apply **maximum likelihood estimation**: maximizing $\ln(P)$ is the same as
minimizing its negative. So we define the loss as the negative log-likelihood
(the binary cross-entropy):

$$
L = -\ln(P).
$$

For gradient descent we need the gradient of $L$ with respect to the weights:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{w}} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w_0} \\[2ex]
\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} \\[2ex]
\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

## Worked example: $\partial L / \partial w_2$

Let $g = g(h^{(i)})$ for brevity, and recall $\dfrac{\partial h^{(i)}}{\partial w_2} = x_2^{(i)}$.

**Derivatives of the two log terms.** Using $g' = g(1-g)$ and the chain rule:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial w_2}\ln(g)
= \frac{1}{g}\, g(1-g)\, x_2^{(i)}
= (1 - g)\, x_2^{(i)},
$$

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial w_2}\ln(1 - g)
= \frac{1}{1 - g}\,\big(-g(1-g)\big)\, x_2^{(i)}
= -\,g\, x_2^{(i)}.
$$

**Assemble the gradient.** Since $L = -\ln(P)$,

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}
= -\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\Big[\, y^{(i)}(1 - g)\,x_2^{(i)} + \big(1 - y^{(i)}\big)\big(-g\big)\,x_2^{(i)} \,\Big].
$$

Expanding the bracket, the cross terms $y^{(i)} g\, x_2^{(i)}$ cancel:

$$
y^{(i)}(1-g)\,x_2^{(i)} - (1 - y^{(i)})\,g\,x_2^{(i)}
= \Big[\, y^{(i)} - \underbrace{y^{(i)}g + y^{(i)}g}_{\text{cancels}} - g \,\Big] x_2^{(i)}
= \big(y^{(i)} - g\big)\,x_2^{(i)}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2}
= -\sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(y^{(i)} - g\big)\, x_2^{(i)}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(g(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \cdot \mathbf{w}) - y^{(i)}\big)\, x_2^{(i)}.
$$

::: {.callout-note title="Same result the long way"}
The same gradient can be obtained by fully expanding
$g = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-h}}$ and cancelling the $e^{-h}$ factors step by step. The
sigmoid-derivative identity $g' = g(1-g)$ used above is just a shortcut to the
identical result:

$$
\frac{y\,e^{-h} - (1 - y)}{1 + e^{-h}}\,x_2
= \frac{y(1 + e^{-h}) - 1}{1 + e^{-h}}\,x_2
= \Big(y - \tfrac{1}{1 + e^{-h}}\Big)x_2
= (y - g)\,x_2 .
$$
:::

## Generalizing to every weight

Nothing above was special to $w_2$ — for $w_1$ the feature is $x_1^{(i)}$, and for
the bias $w_0$ the "feature" is the constant $1$. So for any weight $w_j$:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_j}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(g(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \cdot \mathbf{w}) - y^{(i)}\big)\, x_j^{(i)}.
$$

Stacking these into a vector (with $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} = [\,1,\; x_1^{(i)},\; x_2^{(i)}\,]$) gives the compact form:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{w}}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(g(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \cdot \mathbf{w}) - y^{(i)}\big)\, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}
= X^{\top}\big(g(X\mathbf{w}) - \mathbf{y}\big).
$$

The gradient is simply the **prediction error** $(\hat{y} - y)$ weighted by the
features — the same structural form as linear regression's gradient.

## Gradient-descent update

Finally we update $\mathbf{w}$ iteratively, stepping opposite the gradient with
learning rate $\eta$:

$$
\mathbf{w}^{\text{new}} \;\leftarrow\; \mathbf{w}
\;-\; \eta \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(g(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \cdot \mathbf{w}) - y^{(i)}\big)\, \mathbf{x}^{(i)}.
$$

Repeat until convergence.

::: {.callout-note title="Why derive this by hand"}
In practice you'd reach for a library (`scikit-learn`, etc.) rather than coding
this loop. Working through the derivation is purely to build intuition for
*why* the update rule looks the way it does — and to have a refresher to come
back to later.
:::
